title: Ids counted per kind, links that name it

introduction.text: Steps, notes and contracts each number their ids from 1, and prose links them by kind: `#step:7`, `#note:12`, `#contract:3` (#contract:1, #contract:6). A contract link reads as the contract's name. Older reviews still read: bare `#7` and `[[id]]` resolve and `--check` warns. That fallback breaks once a new step takes an old note's number, so the first tour is about it (#note:1). Then come the link syntax (#contract:2, #contract:4), numbered contracts, and the per-kind next ids that `show.lua` prints (#contract:5, #contract:10). The agent skill was not updated (#note:4).

contracts.name: Links in prose
contracts.why: A link now names its kind: `#step:7`, `#note:12`, `#contract:3`.

before.text:
format 3
  #7               the step or the note whose id is 7 (they share one run of ids)
  other-review#7   the same, in another review
  [[id]]           a contract, by its id (a name), drawn as its name
format 2
  #12              a thread
  #12.3            its step whose id is 3
  other-review#12  the same, in another review

after.text:
format 3
  #step:7               the step whose id is 7
  #note:12              the note whose id is 12
  #contract:3           the contract whose id is 3, drawn as its name
  other-review#note:12  the same, in another review (a contract there is not named)
  #7                    still read: the step or the note that has 7; --check warns to name it.
                        When both have 7 it goes nowhere, and --check reports an error
  [[id]]                still read, for a contract whose id is a name; --check warns
  #tour:1  #Step:1  #note:1.2   no link
format 2
  #12  #12.3  other-review#12   as before; #step:7 is told it is format 3's

prose.text:
Ids are now counted **per kind**, so a bare number no longer says what it points to: step 3 and note 3 can both exist. The kind goes into the link, `#step:3` or `#note:3`.

What a caller sees: every `#7` an agent wrote in an older format 3 review still opens, as long as only one kind has 7 (#step:1). `--check` warns to rewrite it, and reports an error once both kinds have 7. `[[id]]` keeps working for contracts whose id is a name.

What to watch: the readers in the editor were adapted, but two places still **print** bare `#N` labels (#note:6, #note:7), and the skill that teaches agents the syntax was not touched (#note:4).

dependents.text: `link.find` now scans every `#`, not only `#<digit>`, to read a kind before the number. It also has to reject `#note:1.2` and unknown kinds.
A `#contract:3` span takes the contract's name as its text. Links to steps and notes keep their written form.
New scan: `--check` warns on `#tour:1`, a kind no link names.
SKILL.md still teaches `#7` for a step or a note, and `[[id]]` for contracts. An agent following it writes the form `--check` now warns about (#note:4).
A contract page's "touched by" rows list steps as `#3`, the bare form (#note:6).
A note's row starts with `#1`. A user who copies that into a reply writes a bare link that may be ambiguous (#note:7).

contracts.name: thread.Link
contracts.why: A parsed link: `thread` became `id`, and `kind` was added.

prose.text:
`thread` held the number for every link. Now `id` holds it, and `kind` says what it numbers. With no `kind` the link is bare: in format 2 it is a thread, and in format 3 it is an old link (#contract:1). `step` stays, but only format 2's `#12.3` uses it.

Worked case: `link.find 'see other#note:4.'` gives `{ review = 'other', kind = 'note', id = 4 }`. Before, `#4` gave `{ thread = 4 }`.

Anything that built a link table by hand had to rename `thread` to `id`. A grep for `thread =` next to `step =` finds only the go test.

dependents.text: Writes `kind:` between the `#` and the id when there is one.
Reads `l.kind` and `l.id` to name a contract link.
Looks up by `l.kind`. A bare link tries both kinds (#step:8).
Format 2 finds the thread by `l.id`. Before, it used `l.thread`.
The go test's hand-built links read `id =`.

contracts.name: link.follow(l, r, get)
contracts.why: It returns a third value, `wrong`, and may return a target together with a warning.

prose.text:
Before, a target and a `why` never came back together: `why` meant the link went nowhere. Now a bare `#7` that resolves returns the target **and** a `why` that says how to rewrite it. `wrong` marks a `why` that is an error (the link fits two things), as opposed to one that is a tidy-up.

So a caller that treats any `why` as failure would now refuse bare links that still work. Neither caller does that.

dependents.text: It checks `got` first and drops `why` when there is one, so a bare link that resolves still opens.
Reports `why` as an error when `wrong` is set, and as a warning otherwise.

contracts.name: link.to(c)
contracts.why: The link it writes for a conversation names the kind.

before.text:
link.to(c) --> '[[resume]]'     a contract, by its id
           --> '#7'             a format 3 step or note, by its id
           --> '#12', '#12.3'   a format 2 thread, its step

after.text:
link.to(c) --> '#contract:3'    a contract numbered; '[[resume]]' for one named
           --> '#step:7'        a format 3 step
           --> '#note:12'       a format 3 note: one with t.note (#contract:9)
           --> '#12', '#12.3'   a format 2 thread, its step

prose.text:
The signature is unchanged, but every string it returns changed form. Its callers show that string to the user or to the agent, so the change is visible everywhere, including `show.lua`'s list of what waits. That list is how an agent learns which conversation it is answering.

To tell a note from a format 2 thread, it needs `t.note` (#contract:9). Before, both came out as `#id`.

dependents.text: The compose title now reads `Reply in #step:1`.
A step's head shows `#step:1`.
Prints `#contract:1  contract ...`. The show test was adapted.
Prints `#step:1  step ...`.
Prints `#note:2  note ...`.

contracts.name: review.next_id(r, kind)
contracts.why: It gives the next id of the kind asked for. With no kind it gives a note's.

prose.text:
Before, format 3 had one counter shared by steps and notes. Now each of `'step'`, `'note'` and `'contract'` has its own. Leaving `kind` out means a note, or a thread in format 2, so the one old caller is unchanged.

What to watch: in a review written with the shared counter, the next step id can equal an existing note's id. That is where old bare links break (#note:1).

dependents.text: A note the user adds passes no kind and gets the next note id, which is what it should get.
Asks for all three and prints `next ids: step N, note N, contract N`.

contracts.name: Ids in a format 3 review
contracts.why: Steps, notes and contracts each number from 1, and only within their own kind.

before.text:
// every id a format 3 review has
interface Step     { id: number } // from 1; no other step *or note* has it
interface Note     { id: number } // from 1; no other note *or step* has it
interface Contract { id: string } // a name: letters, digits, - _ . ; linked [[id]]

prose.text:
This is a change to data on disk. Every review written before stays valid, because one shared run of ids is still unique within each kind. A review written now can have step 3 and note 3 at once, and it reads as a format error under the old code.

The read path stays lenient: a contract named `resume` still loads. `--check` asks to renumber it, and that changes its read marks and the user's `[[resume]]` links (#note:9).

dependents.text: Checks steps against steps and notes against notes. The shared `own` check is gone.
A format 3 contract id must be a whole number, unless it is a string, which reads with a warning.
The `.seen` key becomes `contract:1`. Renumbering a named contract moves its key from `contract:resume`, so its read marks are lost.
SKILL.md still says "steps and notes share one run of ids" (#note:5).

contracts.name: thread.Contract.id
contracts.why: A contract's id is `integer|string`: a number now, a name in older reviews.

prose.text:
Lookups compare with `==`, so `1` and `"1"` are different contracts to `contract.find` but the same contract to the duplicate check (#step:14). The screen state, the conversation names and `contract.names` all use the id as it is, number or string.

Nothing in the editor turns one into the other, so a reader that kept the id as text, for example from a buffer variable, would miss. The grep finds no such reader.

dependents.text: Type annotation only.
Finds the contract by the id the screen stored, which is a number or a string as it came.
Passes the contract's own id back to `find`.
Keys the names table by the id, so `names[l.id]` works for a numbered contract and `names[id]` for `[[id]]`.
`'contract:' .. c.id` concatenates a number as well as a string.

contracts.name: prose.parse, rows, cut, first_line (…, names)
contracts.why: The prose readers take the contracts' names, so a `#contract:3` link reads as the name.

before.text:
prose.parse(s)
prose.rows(s, width)
prose.cut(s, width, most)
prose.first_line(s)
prose.draw(P, s, width, o)        -- o.names: [[id]] read as [[name]]

after.text:
prose.parse(s, names)             -- names = contract.names(r), optional
prose.rows(s, width, names)
prose.cut(s, width, most, names)
prose.first_line(s, names)
prose.draw(P, s, width, o)        -- o.names: #contract:3 and [[id]] read as the name

prose.text:
`names` is optional and comes last, so no caller broke. A caller that leaves it out shows `#contract:3` as written. Before, it showed `[[id]]` without its brackets.

`cut` has to see the same text that `draw` lays out, or it misjudges whether a folded message runs past its rows. It now resolves names exactly as `draw` does (#step:18).

dependents.text: A message's one-line form shows the contract's name.
Passes the same `names` as the draw just above it.
A note with no title shows its first line with `#contract:3` raw (#note:11).
This briefing view passes no names, so `#contract:3` shows raw (#note:11).
`--check` wants links as written, so not naming them is right here.

contracts.name: thread.note
contracts.why: It marks a format 3 note while it is read. It is never written to disk.

prose.text:
Notes are read as threads. A note and a format 2 thread look the same, but they now link differently (`#note:3` against `#3`), so `link.to` needs a mark. It is set in the two places a format 3 note comes from, read from disk and added by the user, and removed on save.

The risk is a third way of making a note that forgets the mark. That note would link as `#3`, a bare link. Grepping for pushes into `r.notes` finds only those two.

dependents.text: Tells a note from a format 2 thread by the mark.
Marks each note it reads.
Marks a note the user adds.
Copies each note without the mark, so the file never carries it. The test checks `raw.notes[3].note == nil`.

contracts.name: show.lua's line for a review
contracts.why: It prints the next id of each kind, where it printed one shared id.

before.text:
file .threads/three.json · about <diff> · next step or note id 5
  file .threads/old.json · about <diff> · next thread id 5          (format 2)

after.text:
file .threads/three.json · about <diff> · next ids: step 3, note 3, contract 1
  file .threads/old.json · about <diff> · next thread id 5          (format 2)

prose.text: Agents read this line to choose new ids, and it is the only place they get them from. The skill says "`show.lua` prints the next" and still describes one run (#note:5).

dependents.text: Builds the line per format.
The show test expects the new line, and `#step:1` and `#note:2` as the conversations' names.
Still tells the agent that steps and notes share the id it prints (#note:5).

tours.title: Reviews written with one run of ids

nodes.label: one has it: go there, warn to name it
next step id: past steps only

edges.label: gives a step a note's number

steps.title: A bare #7 goes to whichever of step 7 and note 7 exists

text.text:
`follow_three` looks up both kinds. When exactly one has the id, it returns that conversation along with a `why` that says to rewrite the link as `#step:7` or `#note:7`. Before, it tried the note first and then the step, and needed nothing more, because the two could never share a number:

{{chunk:follow-three-old}}

steps.title: When both kinds have the number, the link goes nowhere and --check reports an error

text.text: `follow` returns `wrong = true` for the ambiguous case, and `check` turns that into `fields.bad` in place of `fields.warn`. In the editor, Enter on it opens nothing. `go.follow` returns `false` and the `why`, which is written for the agent ("name which it goes to"), and `wrong` is dropped there.

steps.title: The next step id counts only steps, so in an old review it can take a note's number

text.text:
`next_id(r, 'step')` is `thread.next_step_id(carrier)`, one past the highest step. Take a review written with one run: steps 1 and 2, notes 3 and 4. The next step is 3, which note 3 already has. The test pins exactly that (`{ 3, 5, 1 }` for `shared()`) without checking what it does to `#3`. The old counter counted both:

{{chunk:next-id-body-old}}

steps.title: Steps are no longer checked against notes, so nothing stops the clash

text.text:
`three.parse` keeps one table of step ids and one of note ids. Step 3 next to note 3 is valid now, by design. The shared check it replaces:

{{chunk:three-own-old}}

steps.title: shared() is the fixture renumbered as an old review

text.text: `shared()` takes `three()`, whose steps and notes now each start at 1, and gives the notes 3 and 4 with a bare `#1` in note 3: a review as the old counter wrote it. Every compatibility test reads it.

steps.title: The test covers the fallback on a review that nothing was added to

text.text: It checks that `#1` and `#3` in `shared()` resolve and warn, that `#9` and `#0` go nowhere, and that `#1` in a new review, where step 1 and note 1 both exist, is the error. It never adds a step to `shared()` and then follows its old `#3`. That is the case #note:1 shows breaking.

steps.title: link.find reads a kind only if it is step, note or contract

text.text: `^#(%l+):(%d+)()` anchored at the `#`, then `KIND[kind]`. A kind followed by `.3` or `:3` is dropped, so `#note:12.3` is no link. Lowercase only: `#Step:1` is plain text.

steps.title: A bare number is parsed as before, into id where thread was

text.text: The dotted-number loop is unchanged, now behind `^#%d`. The scan goes over every `#` now, because a kind starts with a letter. The checks on the character before and after the link (`[%w_#/]`, `[%w_]`) still keep out colours, URLs and `a_b#3`.

steps.title: A link with a kind looks only in that kind

text.text: `find` is a table of three lookups: step through the carrier, note through `review.find`, never id 0, which is the carrier's, and contract through `contract.find` and `thread.about`. `#step:9` that goes nowhere says `goes to no step`, naming the kind it looked in.

steps.title: Format 2 rejects a link with a kind and says why

text.text: `#step:7` in a format 2 review returns "is format 3's" rather than looking for a thread 7. That covers `other#note:1` pointing at a format 2 review.

steps.title: link.to writes each conversation's link with its kind

text.text: A numbered contract gives `#contract:3`, a named one keeps `[[id]]`, a carrier's step gives `#step:7`, and a note, known by its `note` mark (#contract:9), gives `#note:12`. Everything else is format 2's `#12` or `#12.3`.

steps.title: --check warns on a kind no link names

text.text: In text that is neither code nor a link, `#(%l+):%d` with an unknown kind warns, so `#tour:1` gets a message. A known kind that `link.find` rejected, `#note:1.2`, gets none (#note:8).

steps.title: The find test covers each kind, another review, and the near misses

text.text: It covers `#step:7`, `#note:12` and `#contract:3` with a full stop after them, `other-review#note:4`, and seven forms that are no link, then the old bare forms with `thread` renamed to `id`. It does not test a kind link inside a URL (`/x#step:1`). The `/` check covers that case as it covered `/notes#12`.

tours.title: Contracts numbered, and read as their name

introduction.text: A contract's id becomes a number (#contract:7). A link to it is drawn as the contract's name and opens its page. A contract with a name for its id still reads, with a warning, and so does `[[id]]`. `--check` now reads contract pages too, though not all of each page (#note:2).

steps.title: A format 3 contract id is a whole number; a name still reads, with a warning

text.text: `parse_id` sends anything that is not a string to `fields.count` (a whole number, 1 or more). A string id keeps the old character check and, in format 3, warns that it should be numbered. Format 2 is unchanged.

steps.title: The duplicate check compares ids as text, so 1 and "1" clash

text.text: `key = tostring(id)`. A numbered 1 and a named `"1"` are reported as one id used twice, even though `#contract:1` and `[[1]]` could tell them apart. That is harmless, and probably what you want.

steps.title: A link to one of this review's contracts is drawn as its name

text.text: `spans_of` replaces the span's text with `names[l.id]` and marks it `contract`, but keeps `link` so Enter still follows it. A link into another review is not named, because `names` is this review's only.

steps.title: names reach spans_of through parse, and through rows from draw

text.text: `parse(s, names)` hands `names` to `spans_of` on every text line, `rows` passes it to `parse`, and `draw` passes `o.names` to `rows`. Before, `names` stopped at `draw`, where `named` rewrote `[[id]]` as text. A link is a span, not text, so it has to be named at parse time.

steps.title: The contract colour takes precedence over the link colour

text.text: A named link has both `link` and `contract` set, so `colour` now checks `contract` first. A `[[id]]` span had only `contract` and is unaffected.

steps.title: Enter on a contract link opens its page

text.text: `go.follow` checks `c.contract` before `c.step`. A contract conversation sits on the carrier, which has steps but no `c.step`, so the order only matters for readability.

steps.title: cut measures prose as draw lays it out, names and all

text.text: `cut` decides whether a folded message is cut short. It now runs the same `named` and `rows(…, names)` that `draw` does, so a long contract name that wraps counts. `first_line` does the same for one-line forms.

steps.title: --check warns on [[id]] in format 3, and on one that names nothing

text.text: A `[[id]]` that finds a contract warns, in format 3, that it should be numbered. One that finds none warns in both formats. Before, an unknown `[[id]]` was never checked at all.

steps.title: --check reads a contract's text and its conversation

text.text: New in this change: links and excerpts in `c.text` and in the agent's messages on a contract are checked. `why`, shape blocks, promises and uses are drawn on the page with links resolved, but they are not checked (#note:2).

steps.title: The named-contract test covers reading, linking and the warnings

text.text: It checks the parse warning, that `link.to` gives `[[resume]]`, the two `--check` warnings (`[[resume]]` and `#tour:`), that the span is drawn as the name, and the id errors for a duplicate `1` and for `0`.

steps.title: The screen test puts the cursor on the drawn name and follows it

text.text: It checks that `#contract:1` shows as `walk.resume(t)` while `#step:1` stays as written, then presses Enter on the name and lands on the page. That proves the link columns follow the replaced text.

tours.title: Each kind's next id, and what marks a note

introduction.text:
`next_id` asks for a kind (#contract:5), `show.lua` prints all three (#contract:10), and a note carries a mark while it is read so it links as a note (#contract:9):

{{diagram:next}}

children.label: next_id(r, 'contract'): past the highest numbered contract

steps.title: next_id counts the kind it is asked for, and a note when asked for none

text.text:
`'note'` and no kind both take the format 2 path, the highest thread id, which in format 3 is the highest note id since the carrier is 0. `'contract'` skips named contracts. Before, there was one counter:

{{chunk:next-id-body-old}}

steps.title: show.lua prints each kind's next id

text.text: `next ids: step 3, note 3, contract 1` in format 3, and `next thread id N` in format 2. This is what an agent reads before choosing an id.

steps.title: Each note read from disk is marked as a note

text.text: `carry` sets `n.note = true` as it lists notes after the carrier. Before, it `list_extend`ed them unmarked.

steps.title: Save writes each note without the mark

text.text: `save` copies each note shallowly and clears `note`, so the mark never reaches the file and the in-memory note keeps it.

steps.title: A note the user adds is marked too

text.text: `add` marks the new thread before appending it to `r.notes`, so `link.to` names it `#note:N` before any reread.

steps.title: The save test checks that a note the user adds gets the next note id and no mark on disk

text.text: After `review.add` and `save`, the new note is id 3 in memory and on disk, after notes 1 and 2, and `raw.notes[3].note` is nil. That covers #step:26 and #step:27 together.

steps.title: The next-ids test covers fresh, shared-run and named-contract reviews

text.text: It checks `{ 3, 3, 1 }` for a fresh review, `{ 3, 5, 1 }` for `shared()`, and `{ 3, 3, 5 }` with contracts `4` and `named`. It does not check that the next step id avoids an existing note's number in `shared()` (#note:1).

notes.title: A step added to an old review takes a note's number and breaks its bare links

prose.text:
In a review written with one shared counter, the next step id (#step:3) is the id of an existing note. From then on, every bare `#N` written for that note fits both kinds and goes nowhere (#step:2):

{{diagram:clash}}

I ran `nvim --headless --clean -l /tmp/review-c-scratch/collide.lua` on a review with steps 1 and 2, notes 3 and 4, and `as #3 says` in note 4. It prints:

- `next step id: 3 next note id: 5`
- before: `#3 -> #note:3`, warned `names no kind`
- with a step 3 added: `#3 -> nowhere`, `is step 3 and note 3 both`, `wrong=true`

The user's own messages are never checked or rewritten, so their bare links break silently. **Fix**: in a review that has bare links, or any review where a step and a note shared ids, continue the next step and note ids past the highest of both. That is the old counter, kept only for old reviews.

messages.label: adds a tour, its first step id 3

notes.title: --check skips links in a contract's why, blocks, promises and uses

prose.text:
The new loop (#step:20) checks `c.text` and the agent's messages. The contract page also draws `why`, each shape block's `text`, each promise and each use's `note` as prose with `names`, so they can hold `#step:9` too. I gave a contract a bad link in each of `why`, `text`, a promise and a block. `--check` reported only the one in `text`:

`warnings = { "the review, contract 1: `#step:8` goes to no step; ..." }`

The fix is in #note:3.

notes.title: --check reads every prose part of a contract's page
SKILL.md says steps and notes share one run of ids

prose.text: This line contradicts #contract:6 and the `next ids: step N, note N, contract N` line `show.lua` now prints (#contract:10). An agent that believes it would pick a step id past the highest note, which is harmless but wastes numbers. It also never learns that contracts are numbered.

notes.title: A contract page lists its steps as bare #3

prose.text: On a contract page, the "touched by" row for a tour lists its steps as `#3 #4`, while the notes under it read `note 1 · ...`. With per-kind ids, `#3` looks like the bare link that `--check` now warns about, and it can also be a note. `link.write { kind = 'step', id = s.id }`, or `step 3`, would match the rest (#contract:1).

notes.title: A note's row is headed #1, which reads as a bare link

prose.text: Format 3 notes go through this head on the review screen, so note 1 shows as `#1  title`. A user replying "as #1 says" writes a bare link, which is ambiguous as soon as step 1 exists. Only the agent's prose is checked, so nobody is told. `note 1` (what `thread.named` says) or `#note:1` would avoid it.

notes.title: #note:1.2 and #Step:1 are plain text with no warning

prose.text: The scan warns only on a kind outside `KINDS`. `#note:1.2` has a known kind, `link.find` rejects it (#step:6), and nothing tells the agent. Neither `#Step:1` nor `#step: 1` matches `%l+:%d` at all. A warning for a known kind that did not become a link ("`#note:1.2` is no link: ...") would catch the likely typos.

notes.title: Should --check tell the agent to renumber a named contract?

prose.text: The warning says "number it, one past the highest contract id". Doing that moves the contract's `.seen` key from `contract:resume` to `contract:1`, so the user's read marks on its conversation are lost. Any `[[resume]]` in the user's own messages then names nothing, and the agent may not edit those. Since a named contract reads fine, should the warning apply only to reviews with no conversation on the contract, or say to leave it when the user has replied there?

notes.title: A contract link reads as its name; step and note links read as written

prose.text: `#contract:3` is drawn as `walk.resume(t)`, while `#step:7` stays `#step:7` (#step:15). A contract has a name that says more than its number, and steps and notes have titles too long to inline. The cost: the text the user sees differs from the text in the file, so searching the buffer for `#contract:3` finds nothing. Links into another review are not named. Agree?

notes.title: Pass names to the prose readers that still show #contract:3 raw

prose.text: Some prose readers pass no `names` (#contract:8): this tour briefing, the title of a note with none (`draw/thread.lua:45`), `draw/step.lua:134`, `draw/files.lua:164`, and the code marks. There a contract link reads `#contract:3`, where the review screen shows the name. Tour briefings are where contracts get linked most. Before, these showed `[[id]]` as the bare id, so this is no regression, only an inconsistency.

notes.title: The note-tours error still says `#id` links

prose.text: "a note says where with excerpts, notes and `#id` links" is what the agent reads. `#step:7` links would match the new syntax.
`make test` in a clone at 3992d19: `250 tests, 0 failed`. The changed specs are `three_spec`, `prose_spec` and `go_spec`. The gaps in them are in #step:5 and #step:28.

chunks.to: ---@field step integer|nil  format 2's: its thread's step with this id
return M.write { id = c.thread.id, step = c.step and c.step.id }

chunks.from: local kind, n, e = s:match('^#(%l+):(%d+)()', hash)

chunks.to: l = #parts <= 2 and { id = parts[1], step = parts[2] } or nil
